before.question: What are the maximum absolute and relative components of the materiality threshold for retail past-due credit obligations?
before.expected_answer: Absolute component: at most EUR 100 (or national-currency equivalent) for the sum of amounts past due; relative component: between 0% and 2.5% of total on-balance exposures to the obligor, set at 1% unless the competent authority justifies otherwise. Both must be exceeded for the obligation to be material. Non-retail absolute component is at most EUR 500.
before.author: claude-draft
before.notes: Checked in source text and reviewed 2026-10-27.

after.question: What are the maximum absolute and relative components of the materiality threshold for retail past-due credit obligations?
after.expected_answer: The authority-set absolute component must not exceed EUR 100 (or its national-currency equivalent). The relative component is between 0% and 2.5%, normally 1% where the authority considers that reasonable. Its denominator is the institution's, parent's and subsidiaries' total on-balance-sheet exposures to the obligor, excluding equity exposures. Both components must be exceeded for the material past-due criterion; the applicable consecutive-day period must also be met.
after.author: claude-draft
after.notes: Checked in source text and reviewed 2026-10-27. Source audit revision 2026-11-11 (Codex; not practitioner sign-off). Grading criteria and assumptions are in grading_notes.
after.grading_notes: The non-retail EUR 500 cap is optional context, not a required fact for this retail question. These are RTS settings/caps, not an assertion of the actual setting in every jurisdiction.

before.question: What is the minimum probation period before a defaulted exposure (not under distressed restructuring) can be reclassified as non-defaulted?
before.expected_answer: At least 3 months after the conditions of Art. 178(1)(b) and 178(3) cease to be met, taking into account the obligor's behaviour and financial situation during that period.
before.author: claude-draft
before.notes: Checked in source text and reviewed 2026-10-27. Alternatives accepted 2026-10-27 (retrieval review).

after.question: What is the minimum probation period before a defaulted exposure (not under distressed restructuring) can be reclassified as non-defaulted?
after.expected_answer: At least three months after the conditions in CRR Articles 178(1)(b) and 178(3) cease to be met. This is a minimum probation period, not automatic cure; the other reclassification conditions must also be satisfied.
after.author: claude-draft
after.notes: Checked in source text and reviewed 2026-10-27. Alternatives accepted 2026-10-27 (retrieval review). Source audit revision 2026-11-11 (Codex; not practitioner sign-off). Grading criteria and assumptions are in grading_notes.
after.grading_notes: Required: the three-month minimum and its start. Details of the broader cure assessment are optional. ECB 170/172 are not standalone equivalents for the minimum-period fact.

before.question: How long is the probation period for a defaulted exposure subject to distressed restructuring?
before.expected_answer: At least 1 year from the latest of: (a) extending the restructuring measures, (b) the exposure being classified as defaulted, (c) the end of the grace period in the restructuring arrangements. Reclassification also requires, among others, a material payment during that period, no past-due amounts and no remaining concerns about full repayment.
before.author: claude-draft
before.notes: Checked in source text and reviewed 2026-10-27. Alternatives accepted 2026-10-27 (retrieval review).

after.expected_answer: At least 1 year from the latest of: (a) extending the restructuring measures, (b) the exposure being classified as defaulted, (c) the end of the grace period in the restructuring arrangements. Reclassification also requires, among others, a material payment during that period, no past-due amounts and no remaining concerns about full repayment.

before.question: What minimum length of historical observation period is required for PD estimation?
before.expected_answer: At least five years for at least one data source, for both non-retail (Art. 180(1)(h)) and retail (Art. 180(2)(e)) exposures.
before.author: claude-draft
before.notes: Checked in source text and reviewed 2026-10-27.

after.question: What minimum length of historical observation period is required for PD estimation?
after.expected_answer: Normally at least five years for at least one data source, using a longer available period where relevant and a representative mix of good and bad years. At IRB implementation, the competent authority may permit relevant data covering two years, then an additional year each year until five years is covered. For non-retail exposures this exception is restricted to institutions without permission to use own LGD estimates or IRB-CCF; the retail implementation exception is also subject to authority permission.
after.author: claude-draft

before.expected_answer: 55% for 1 January to 31 December 2026 (phase-in: 50% 2025, 55% 2026, 60% 2027, 65% 2028, 70% 2029; end state x = 72.5% under Art. 92(3)). A Member State may decide that the un-floored total risk exposure amount applies at solo level.
before.author: claude-draft
before.notes: Checked in source text and reviewed 2026-10-27.

before.question: A bank has A-IRB permission. Can it use its own LGD and CCF estimates for a corporate group with EUR 800 million consolidated sales?
before.expected_answer: No. The obligor is a large corporate (sales > EUR 500m), and under CRR3 exposures to large corporates (not in the specialised lending class) must use the supervisory LGD values of Art. 161(1) and SA-CCFs, i.e. F-IRB treatment.
before.author: claude-draft
before.notes: Art. 151(8)(c) checked in text. Needs definition lookup + scope rule.

after.question: An A-IRB bank has an exposure classified as general corporate, not specialised lending, to a non-financial corporate group with EUR 800 million consolidated sales measured under CRR Article 142(1)(5a). May it use own LGD and CCF estimates for that exposure?
after.expected_answer: No. The obligor is a large corporate (sales > EUR 500m), and under CRR3 exposures to large corporates (not in the specialised lending class) must use the supervisory LGD values of Art. 161(1) and SA-CCFs, i.e. F-IRB treatment.
after.author: claude-draft

before.question: What does the regulatory framework require for downturn LGD, and what applies if no downturn can be observed in the bank's data?
before.expected_answer: Institutions must use LGD estimates appropriate for an economic downturn where more conservative than the long-run average (Art. 181(1)(b)). The RTS specifies how the downturn period is identified; its duration (Art. 4) is based on the most severe 12-month values of the economic indicators, and recital 14 states a downturn period should last at least 12 months. Where neither observed nor estimated downturn impact is available, the institution must include a strictly positive Category A MoC, and the final downturn LGD including MoC must be at least min(long-run average LGD + 15 percentage points, 105%).
before.author: claude-draft
before.notes: Checked in source text and reviewed 2026-10-27. Note: 105% bounds the floor (min of LRA+15pp and 105%).

after.question: What does the regulatory framework require for downturn LGD, and what applies if no downturn can be observed in the bank's data?
after.expected_answer: Article 181(1)(b) requires downturn-appropriate LGD when more conservative than the long-run average. Identify downturn periods using the relevant economic indicators and their most severe 12-month values; the duration is at least 12 months and may be longer. Where observed loss data cannot support calibration, first consider estimating the downturn impact using Section 6 of the EBA downturn guidelines. Only where neither observed-impact nor Section 6 calibration is possible may the paragraph-36 fallback be used: justify that inability to the competent authority, include a strictly positive Category A MoC for missing data, and ensure final downturn LGD including MoC is at least min(long-run average LGD + 15 percentage points, 105%). No observed impact, no relevant data, and inability to estimate impact are different cases.
after.author: claude-draft
after.notes: Checked in source text and reviewed 2026-10-27. Note: 105% bounds the floor (min of LRA+15pp and 105%). Source audit revision 2026-11-11 (Codex; not practitioner sign-off). Grading criteria and assumptions are in grading_notes.
after.grading_notes: Required: the normal downturn rule, consideration of estimated-impact calibration before the final fallback, and the conditional fallback safeguards. Do not infer a flat 15-point add-on whenever a bank lacks observed downturn data.

before.question: An A-IRB bank recognises financial collateral in its own LGD estimates for other retail exposures. Which CRR requirements and floors apply?
before.expected_answer: It must consider the dependence between the risk of the obligor and that of the funded credit protection or its provider (Art. 181(1)(c)), and treat currency mismatches between the obligation and the collateral conservatively (Art. 181(1)(d)). The LGD input floor for other retail exposures secured by financial collateral is 0% (Art. 164(4), Table 1), compared with 30% if unsecured.
before.author: claude-draft
before.notes: Checked in source text and reviewed 2026-10-27. Replaces the earlier guarantee question.

after.question: An A-IRB bank recognises eligible financial collateral that fully secures an other-retail exposure after the relevant volatility and currency adjustments. Which CRR dependence/currency requirements and LGD input floor apply?
after.expected_answer: Consider dependence between the obligor and the funded protection or provider, and address significant dependence conservatively (Article 181(1)(c)). Treat currency mismatches conservatively in LGD (Article 181(1)(d)). The fully eligible secured floor is 0%, compared with 30% for unsecured other-retail exposures (Article 164(4)); full coverage after the relevant adjustments is required under Article 164(4a). Partially secured exposures instead use a weighted floor.
after.author: claude-draft
after.notes: Checked in source text and reviewed 2026-10-27. Replaces the earlier guarantee question. Source audit revision 2026-11-11 (Codex; not practitioner sign-off). Grading criteria and assumptions are in grading_notes.
after.grading_notes: The question supplies full eligible adjusted coverage. Details of the partial-collateral formula are optional context.

before.question: What back-testing must an IRB bank perform on PD estimates, and how are the results reported to the ECB?
before.expected_answer: Under Art. 185(b) the bank must regularly compare realised default rates with estimated PDs for each grade and analyse deviations outside the expected range, and do the same for own LGD and CCF estimates. Per the ECB instructions of February 2019, significant institutions submit the results with their annual validation report, using the ECB templates; tests include discriminatory power (e.g. AUC). The answer should note the instructions predate CRR3.
before.author: claude-draft
before.notes: Checked in source text and reviewed 2026-10-27. Source is the Feb 2019 version; answer should state the date.

after.question: For an IRB institution covered by the ECB reporting Decision referred to in the February 2019 validation-reporting instructions, what PD back-testing does CRR Article 185(b) require, and how are the results submitted under Section 2.2 of those instructions?
after.expected_answer: Regularly compare realised default rates with estimated PDs for each grade and analyse deviations outside the expected range. Use historical data covering as long a period as possible, document methods/data, and update the analysis and documentation at least annually; analogous comparisons apply to own LGD/CCF estimates. Under Section 2.2 of the February 2019 instructions, institutions covered by the Decision submit validation-exercise results to the ECB using its templates when submitting their annual internal-validation report.
after.author: claude-draft
after.notes: Checked in source text and reviewed 2026-10-27. Source is the Feb 2019 version; answer should state the date. Source audit revision 2026-11-11 (Codex; not practitioner sign-off). Grading criteria and assumptions are in grading_notes.
after.grading_notes: The reporting obligation is limited to institutions covered by the referenced Decision. AUC is not established by Section 2.2 and is not a required scoring fact. The instruction version is explicitly historical.

before.question: Which floors constrain the capital requirement of an IRB retail mortgage portfolio in 2026?
before.expected_answer: Input floors apply per exposure: PD at least 0.05% (retail other than QRRE revolvers) and LGD at least 5% for retail exposures secured by residential property. The output floor (factor 55% in 2026) applies to the institution's total risk exposure amount, not to the portfolio alone, comparing it with the standardised approach (where mortgages use 20% up to 55% of property value); a Member State may exempt the solo level.
before.author: claude-draft
before.notes: Checked in source text and reviewed 2026-10-27.

after.question: Which input and output floors constrain an ordinary IRB retail residential-mortgage portfolio in 2026, assuming no eligible sovereign/central-bank guarantee under Article 159a and an institution subject to the output floor without the group/solo derogation?
after.expected_answer: Per exposure, the normal PD input floor is 0.05% for retail exposures other than QRRE revolvers and the residential-property LGD input floor is 5%. In 2026 the output-floor factor is 55%, applied to the institution's total risk exposure amount by comparison with its standardised total, not independently to this portfolio. Input floors and the institution-wide output floor are distinct constraints.
after.author: claude-draft
after.notes: Checked in source text and reviewed 2026-10-27. Source audit revision 2026-11-11 (Codex; not practitioner sign-off). Grading criteria and assumptions are in grading_notes.

before.question: Does the ECB guide to internal models apply to a less significant institution supervised by its national competent authority?
before.expected_answer: The guide explains how the ECB understands and applies the CRR when it grants internal-model permissions, i.e. for the institutions it supervises directly (significant institutions). It does not address LSIs: saying the guide (or the passages) does not cover or address LSIs is a correct answer. It is not law and does not overrule EU or national law. For an LSI the binding requirements remain the CRR, RTS and EBA guidelines as applied by its national competent authority; any use of the guide by NCAs is outside this corpus.
before.author: claude-draft
before.notes: Checked in source text and reviewed 2026-10-27. Reference reworded 2026-10-29: 'does not address / passages do not say' phrasing accepted.

after.question: What do paragraphs 1-3 of the ECB guide's foreword establish about its legal force and purpose, and do those passages alone establish whether an NCA-supervised less significant institution must follow the guide?
after.expected_answer: They explain the ECB's understanding of the applicable rules and its approach to assessing internal-model permissions, and support consistency among supervisory teams. The guide does not replace or overrule EU or national law. Those passages alone do not establish an obligation for an NCA-supervised LSI to follow the guide; that requires further evidence about the applicable supervisory framework.
after.author: claude-draft
after.notes: Checked in source text and reviewed 2026-10-27. Reference reworded 2026-10-29: 'does not address / passages do not say' phrasing accepted. Source audit revision 2026-11-11 (Codex; not practitioner sign-off). Grading criteria and assumptions are in grading_notes.

before.question: For which exposures may an institution use its own IRB conversion factors (IRB-CCF) under CRR3?
before.expected_answer: Only, with permission, for undrawn revolving commitments under the IRB approach that would not receive a 100% SA-CCF under the standardised approach; SA-CCFs apply to all other off-balance-sheet items, in particular undrawn non-revolving commitments, and where the IRB-CCF requirements are not met.
before.author: claude-draft
before.notes: Checked in source text 2026-10-27.

after.question: For which exposures may an institution use its own IRB conversion factors (IRB-CCF) under CRR3?

Article 151(8) also limits exposure-class eligibility: institution exposures, other financial-sector entities and large corporates outside specialised lending must use SA-CCFs. SA-CCFs also apply to the other off-balance-sheet items, particularly non-revolving undrawn commitments, and where permission or minimum requirements are absent.

before.author: claude-draft
before.notes: Checked in source text 2026-10-27 (full passage read).

after.question: How should the observed average default rate be calculated for PD calibration?
after.expected_answer: As the arithmetic average of all one-year default rates calculated per paras. 73-76; for retail PD models, a weighted average of one-year default rates may be used where the institution does not give equal importance to historic data because more recent data is a better predictor of losses (Art. 180(2)(e) CRR).

before.question: When is a past-due situation 'technical', and how is it treated?
before.expected_answer: Only where the defaulted status resulted from: (a) the institution's data or system error (incl. manual errors in standardised processes, not wrong credit decisions); (b) non-, defective or late execution of a payment ordered by the obligor, or payment system failure; (c) a time lag between receipt and allocation of a payment made before day 90; (d) for on-balance factoring, a materiality threshold breach where no receivable is more than 30 days past due. Technical past due situations are not defaults and errors must be rectified as soon as possible.
before.author: claude-draft
before.notes: Checked in source text 2026-10-27 (full passage read).

after.question: Under the original 2016 text of EBA/GL/2016/07, before the amendments applying from 19 October 2026, which situations were treated as technical past due and how were they handled?
after.expected_answer: Only where the defaulted status resulted from: (a) the institution's data or system error (incl. manual errors in standardised processes, not wrong credit decisions); (b) non-, defective or late execution of a payment ordered by the obligor, or payment system failure; (c) a time lag between receipt and allocation of a payment made before day 90; (d) for on-balance factoring, a materiality threshold breach where no receivable is more than 30 days past due. Technical past due situations are not defaults and errors must be rectified as soon as possible.
after.author: claude-draft
after.notes: Checked in source text 2026-10-27 (full passage read). Source audit revision 2026-11-11 (Codex; not practitioner sign-off). Grading criteria and assumptions are in grading_notes.
after.grading_notes: Historical source-comprehension question, not current-law guidance. The registered corpus contains the original 2016 text, whose factoring limb uses 30 days. EBA/GL/2026/05 replaces that limb with a 90-day rule and additional cases; a current-rule answer must not be scored against this historical reference. Remove or replace this question when introducing an updated-current-law-only dataset.

before.question: How should LGD be set for a defaulted retail exposure under A-IRB, and when may the ELBE ignore current conditions?
before.expected_answer: LGD in-default = ELBE plus the increase in loss rate from possible additional unexpected losses during recovery (Art. 181(1)(h)); the ELBE equals the long-run average LGD without further adjustment where the model has a macroeconomic driver, a material risk driver is sensitive to economic conditions, or realised LGDs are not sensitive to the cycle (EBA GL para. 184).
before.author: claude-draft
before.notes: Checked in source text 2026-10-27. ECB guide (Credit risk) para. 309 accepted as alternative.

after.question: How is LGD in-default set for a defaulted retail exposure under own LGD estimates, and when does EBA paragraph 184 require no additional adjustment of the ELBE basis for current economic conditions?
after.expected_answer: LGD in-default is ELBE plus the estimated increase in loss rate from possible additional unexpected losses during recovery. Under EBA paragraph 184, ELBE is estimated on the long-run average LGD basis without a further current-conditions adjustment where the model directly includes a macroeconomic risk driver, a material risk driver is sensitive to economic conditions, or realised LGD for defaulted exposures is insensitive to the relevant economic factors. The first two cases capture conditions through the model; they do not permit ignoring economic conditions.
after.author: claude-draft
after.notes: Checked in source text 2026-10-27. ECB guide (Credit risk) para. 309 accepted as alternative. Source audit revision 2026-11-11 (Codex; not practitioner sign-off). Grading criteria and assumptions are in grading_notes.
after.grading_notes: No additional adjustment is different from ignoring current conditions. Accept explanations that the model already reflects the cycle.

before.question: How is an economic downturn period identified for downturn LGD purposes?
before.expected_answer: Using the relevant economic indicators (GDP, unemployment, aggregate default rates/losses, plus sector or house-price indicators by exposure type), examined over a 20-year time span; the downturn period is based on the most severe 12-month values and lasts at least 12 months.
before.author: claude-draft
before.notes: Checked in source text 2026-10-27.

after.question: How is an economic downturn period identified for downturn LGD purposes?
after.expected_answer: Use the relevant indicators by exposure type, including GDP, unemployment and available aggregate default rates/losses, plus appropriate sector/property and other relevant indicators. Examine a 20-year historical window ending at identification, extending it when its variability is not representative of the likely future range. Identify the most severe 12-month indicator values and set a downturn period of at least 12 months, longer where needed to cover related prolonged severity or adjacent peaks/troughs.
after.author: claude-draft
after.notes: Checked in source text 2026-10-27. Source audit revision 2026-11-11 (Codex; not practitioner sign-off). Grading criteria and assumptions are in grading_notes.
after.grading_notes: Required: relevant indicators, the 20-year rule with its representativeness exception, and the minimum rather than fixed 12-month duration.

before.question: How does an A-IRB bank recognise a guarantee in its PD or LGD estimates, and which requirements must the guarantee meet?
before.expected_answer: It recognises unfunded credit protection under Chapter 3 and must comply with Art. 183 (Chapter 4 applies only where Chapter 3 requires it), per EBA Q&A 2016_2593. Art. 183(1) requires clearly specified criteria for recognised guarantors, the obligor rules of Arts. 171-173 for guarantors, and a guarantee that is written, non-cancellable and non-changeable by the guarantor, in force until the obligation is satisfied, legally enforceable, and unconditional.
before.author: claude-draft
before.notes: Reviewed 2026-11-05: kept to test whether the agent consults EBA Q&As (reached via get_qa, not in default search).

after.question: How does an A-IRB bank recognise a guarantee in its PD or LGD estimates, and which requirements must the guarantee meet?
after.expected_answer: Under CRR Article 108(3), Chapter 3 recognition of unfunded credit protection requires the institution to use own LGD estimates for both the original exposure and comparable direct exposures to the protection provider. In that case, Articles 160(4) and 161(3) permit recognition in PD or LGD in accordance with Article 183; in other cases Article 108(3) directs recognition under Chapter 4. Article 183(1) requires clearly specified recognised-guarantor criteria, the relevant obligor-rating rules for guarantors, and a written, non-cancellable/non-changeable, enforceable guarantee covering the specified amount and tenor until satisfaction, which meets the unconditionality requirements.
after.author: claude-draft
after.notes: Reviewed 2026-11-05: kept to test whether the agent consults EBA Q&As (reached via get_qa, not in default search). Source audit revision 2026-11-11 (Codex; not practitioner sign-off). Grading criteria and assumptions are in grading_notes.
after.grading_notes: Do not apply the historical Q&A 2016_2593 as an unconditional current Chapter-3-only rule. The comparable guarantor exposure's own-LGD treatment matters. Nuances of permitted guarantee clauses are valid optional detail.

before.question: How is effective maturity M treated without own LGD estimates compared with when own LGD estimates are used?
before.expected_answer: Without own LGD estimates M is 2,5 years (0,5 years for securities financing transactions) or, alternatively, calculated as in Art. 162(2), applied consistently (Art. 162(1)). With own LGD estimates M is calculated per Art. 162(2) (e.g. cash-flow weighted, or the maximum remaining time with a one-year floor) and is no greater than five years.
before.author: claude-draft
before.notes: Checked in source text 2026-11-05; reviewed.

after.question: How is effective maturity M treated without own LGD estimates compared with when own LGD estimates are used?
after.expected_answer: Without own LGD estimates, apply consistently either M of 2.5 years (0.5 for securities financing transactions) or the calculation under Article 162(2). With own LGD estimates, calculate M under Article 162(2), subject to paragraphs 3-5; normally M is capped at five years, with the express Article 384(2) exception. Special short-term/netting cases have their own floors, and Article 162(4) permits an option for qualifying EU non-large corporates. A one-year floor and five-year cap are not universal for every transaction.
after.author: claude-draft
after.notes: Checked in source text 2026-11-05; reviewed. Source audit revision 2026-11-11 (Codex; not practitioner sign-off). Grading criteria and assumptions are in grading_notes.
after.grading_notes: Required: consistent fixed-or-calculated treatment without own LGD, calculated treatment with own LGD, and qualified rather than universal limits. Exhaustive listing of short-term cases is optional.

before.question: How does the capital treatment of a residential mortgage differ between the CRR3 standardised approach and the A-IRB approach for retail?
before.expected_answer: SA: the part of the exposure up to 55% of the property value gets a 20% risk weight (loan-splitting, reduced for more senior liens not held by the institution) (Art. 125(1)). A-IRB retail: own PD and LGD estimates, subject to input floors of 0,05% PD (Art. 163(1)(b)) and 5% LGD for retail exposures secured by residential property (Art. 164(4)).
before.author: claude-draft
before.notes: Checked in source text 2026-11-05; reviewed: Art. 164(4) Table 1 'Retail exposure secured by residential property 5 %'.

after.question: Compare CRR3 SA and own-estimate IRB treatment of an ordinary retail residential mortgage eligible for Article 125(1), assuming a sole first lien, no national override and no eligible sovereign guarantee under Article 159a.
after.expected_answer: SA applies the 20% loan-splitting risk weight to the part up to 55% of property value under Article 125(1); any remainder is treated as an unsecured exposure to the counterparty. Retail IRB uses own PD/LGD estimates in the relevant formula, subject under the stated assumptions to the 0.05% PD floor and 5% residential-property LGD floor. These are parameter floors, not a 5% risk weight or capital ratio.
after.author: claude-draft
after.notes: Checked in source text 2026-11-05; reviewed: Art. 164(4) Table 1 'Retail exposure secured by residential property 5 %'. Source audit revision 2026-11-11 (Codex; not practitioner sign-off). Grading criteria and assumptions are in grading_notes.
after.grading_notes: The question supplies eligibility and excludes the relevant national/guarantee branches. Required: distinguish the SA risk weight from IRB parameter floors; do not require a calculation without necessary loan/model inputs.

before.question: What must the impact analysis cover when calibrating downturn LGD based on the observed impact of a downturn period?
before.expected_answer: An analysis of the impact of the downturn period on the loss data of the calibration segment, at a minimum including evidence of elevated realised LGDs driven by the downturn period, with realised LGDs averaged over all defaults of a given year (closed or past the maximum recovery time) and incomplete recoveries taken into account (para. 27); downturn LGD is then calibrated with a methodology coherent with that evidence (para. 28).
before.author: claude-draft
before.notes: Checked in source text 2026-11-05; reviewed (para. 27(a)(i) truncated in display; key elements above).

after.question: What must the impact analysis cover when calibrating downturn LGD based on the observed impact of a downturn period?
after.expected_answer: For the calibration segment, paragraph 27(a) requires examining: (i) elevated realised LGDs, including annual default cohorts and incomplete-recovery patterns; (ii) reduced annual recoveries by relevant recovery source, with/without repossessions where applicable; (iii) reduced proportions of defaults returning to non-default within an appropriate fixed horizon; and (iv) increased time in default. Use as many sufficiently supported time points as possible, merge consecutive years where sparse data makes that useful, and consider lags between the downturn and observed losses. Paragraph 28 requires the calibration method to be coherent with that evidence.
after.author: claude-draft
after.notes: Checked in source text 2026-11-05; reviewed (para. 27(a)(i) truncated in display; key elements above). Source audit revision 2026-11-11 (Codex; not practitioner sign-off). Grading criteria and assumptions are in grading_notes.
after.grading_notes: Required: all four minimum evidence dimensions and relevant data/lag considerations. Do not treat elevated LGD alone as the complete minimum impact analysis.

before.question: For a retail obligor with individual and joint credit obligations, how is materiality assessed when one individual obligation is late?
before.expected_answer: The materiality threshold of Art. 178(2)(d) is applied to all individual credit obligations of that obligor, without the joint credit obligations with others; if breached, all individual exposures to the obligor are defaulted (para. 105).
before.author: claude-draft
before.notes: Checked in source text 2026-11-05; reviewed.

after.question: For a retail obligor where default is applied at obligor level, how is materiality assessed when an individual credit obligation is late, and does crossing materiality alone immediately put all individual exposures in past-due default?
after.expected_answer: Assess the threshold on the obligor's individual credit obligations, excluding joint credit obligations with other persons/entities (EBA paragraph 105). Crossing materiality alone is not immediate past-due default: the applicable consecutive-day criterion in CRR Article 178(1)(b) must also be met. Once that individual-obligor default criterion is met, all its individual exposures are treated as defaulted; separate unlikeliness-to-pay triggers remain relevant.
after.author: claude-draft
after.notes: Checked in source text 2026-11-05; reviewed. Source audit revision 2026-11-11 (Codex; not practitioner sign-off). Grading criteria and assumptions are in grading_notes.
after.grading_notes: Separate materiality aggregation from the time/default trigger. The question explicitly supplies obligor-level application and does not ask for facility-level contagion rules.

before.question: How does the ECB's validation reporting distinguish major from severe deficiencies?
before.expected_answer: By the potential RWEA impact: major deficiencies indicate a significant bias, e.g. an impact of at least ±5% but below ±10%; severe deficiencies indicate a severe bias, e.g. an impact of ±10% or more. The other grades are adequate with no deficiencies and adequate with minor deficiencies.
before.author: claude-draft
before.notes: Checked in source text 2026-11-05; reviewed (Section 2.4.2 Validation information).

after.question: In Section 2.4.2 of the ECB's February 2019 validation-reporting instructions, what illustrative potential RWEA-impact bands distinguish major from severe deficiencies?
after.expected_answer: The illustrative major-deficiency band is an impact magnitude of at least 5% but below 10%; the severe-deficiency example is 10% or more. The classification concerns significant/severe bias in risk-parameter estimates: these are illustrative potential-impact examples, not an exclusive automatic legal test based only on a percentage.
after.author: claude-draft
after.notes: Checked in source text 2026-11-05; reviewed (Section 2.4.2 Validation information). Source audit revision 2026-11-11 (Codex; not practitioner sign-off). Grading criteria and assumptions are in grading_notes.
after.grading_notes: Require the section as well as the list-item/paragraph number. Unrelated PD/LGD/CCF statistics numbered 3 or 4 must receive no citation credit. The other two grades are optional context.
